Drawing cash from a fund in a non-registered account: how much of each withdrawal is taxed, and why the share rises over time

Split each redemption from a non-registered mutual fund into returned cost, untaxed gain and taxable gain, using CRA’s average-cost rule. Compare the tax on the same withdrawal from a TFSA, an RRSP or RRIF and a fund with little cost base left, and follow the cost base over 20 years of withdrawals.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Tax on cash withdrawn from a fund in a non-registered account

The fund starts at $300,000 with an adjusted cost base of $200,000. $18,000 is redeemed at the start of the first year, rising 2% a year. Each redemption uses the average cost per unit, so only the part above cost is a capital gain, and half of that gain is taxed at the combined 29.65% marginal rate (20.5% federal plus 9.15% provincial or territorial). Units then grow 4% a year and distributions of 1.5% a year are reinvested and taxed at the full marginal rate, a conservative simplification: eligible dividends and capital gains distributions would be taxed less. Tax is paid from the redeemed cash. Returns are hypothetical, not a forecast, and this is not a personal tax calculation.

The central idea

Redeeming fund units in a non-registered account is not fully taxed: part of each withdrawal returns your own cost, and only half of the gain is taxable. That makes early withdrawals light on tax. As withdrawals continue and the fund grows, the cost base shrinks and the taxable share rises, while reinvested distributions are taxed every year whether or not any units are sold.

01

A withdrawal is not the same thing as income

Many people approaching retirement hold part of their savings in mutual funds in an ordinary, non-registered account, often because their TFSA and RRSP room was already used. When they start drawing cash from it, a common worry is that every dollar taken out will be added to taxable income, as it would be from an RRSP or RRIF. It is not.

CRA describes two separate ways a mutual fund in a non-registered account is taxed. While you own the units, the distributions the fund pays are taxable each year, even when they are reinvested in more units. When you sell or redeem units, you are taxed on the gain, if any, usually as a capital gain. A redemption therefore has three parts: your own cost coming back, which is not taxed; half of the gain, which is left out of income; and the other half of the gain, which is taxed at your marginal rate.

The fund itself has no special tax status; a fund held in a TFSA or RRSP follows that account’s rules instead. This guide is about the non-registered case.

02

The first year, step by step

The default fund is worth CAD 300,000 and has an adjusted cost base (ACB) of CAD 200,000: the total paid for the units, including reinvested distributions. The investor redeems CAD 18,000 at the start of the year.

  • Cost returned: CRA treats units of the same fund series as identical property, so the ACB of the units sold is their share of the average cost. CAD 18,000 is 6% of the fund’s value, so it carries 6% of the ACB, CAD 12,000.
  • Capital gain: CAD 18,000 − CAD 12,000 = CAD 6,000, a third of the withdrawal.
  • Taxable capital gain: half of CAD 6,000, CAD 3,000, is added to income.
  • Tax: at a combined 29.65% marginal rate, CAD 889.50. That is 4.9% of the cash redeemed.

The 29.65% default is the 2026 federal rate of 20.5% plus Ontario’s 9.15%, which together apply to taxable income between about CAD 58,523 and CAD 107,785 in 2026 according to CRA’s rate tables. Your rate depends on your income and province, so change the two inputs; Ontario’s surtax, credits and income-tested benefits are not modeled.

The fund also pays distributions of 1.5% a year on the remaining CAD 282,000, CAD 4,230, which are reinvested. The model taxes them at the full marginal rate, CAD 1,254.20, which is conservative: distributions of eligible dividends or capital gains would be taxed less, as the fund income-type guide shows. After both amounts, about CAD 15,856 of the CAD 18,000 is left to spend if the tax is paid from it.

03

The same withdrawal from different accounts

The first chart compares the tax on the same CAD 18,000 at the same 29.65% rate. A TFSA withdrawal is not taxed. Non-registered units bought recently, with a cost near their value, produce almost no gain. With the entered cost base the tax is CAD 889.50. If the units had no cost base left, the whole CAD 18,000 would be gain and the tax would be CAD 2,668.50. An RRSP or RRIF withdrawal is fully taxable, CAD 5,337 at this rate.

Two cautions keep this from being a ranking of accounts. The RRSP contributions were deducted from income when they were made, so taxing the withdrawal completes a deal that began with a refund; the RRSP and TFSA timing guide compares the full cycle. And the RRSP cash flow differs: for a lump-sum withdrawal, CRA says the institution withholds tax at source, 30% outside Quebec on an amount over CAD 15,000, which may be more or less than the final tax, as the withholding guide explains. Non-registered redemptions have no such withholding, so the tax is settled with the return or through instalments.

04

Why the taxable share keeps rising

The second and third charts follow the plan for 20 years, with the withdrawal rising 2% a year and units growing 4% a year after fund costs. Each redemption removes cost base in proportion to value, and growth adds value but not cost. Reinvested distributions add to both. Over time the ACB falls behind the market value, so each dollar redeemed carries less cost and more gain.

In year 1, a third of the redemption is gain. By year 20 the redemption has grown to about CAD 26,223 and about 58.5% of it is gain; the tax on that year’s redemption is about CAD 2,274, plus about CAD 415 on that year’s distributions. Over the 20 years, CAD 437,353 is redeemed and total tax is about CAD 50,674: CAD 31,605 on redemption gains and CAD 19,069 on distributions. That is about 11.6% of the cash redeemed, far below the 29.65% that would apply if every dollar were income.

The fund still holds about CAD 98,468 at the end, with an ACB of about CAD 40,150. The tax on that unrealized gain, about CAD 8,646 at the same rate, has been deferred, not avoided: gains are taxed when units are sold or are considered to be sold (a deemed disposition). The gain-timing guide values what deferral is worth. Extend the plan to 25 years and the default fund runs out in year 24: lower tax does not make a withdrawal rate sustainable.

05

Cost base and growth matter more than the withdrawal itself

The heatmap reruns the 20-year plan for starting cost bases from 100% to 0% of value and unit growth from 0% to 8% a year. A fund bought recently with no growth pays about 3.2% of its withdrawals in tax, all of it on distributions. A fund with no cost base left that grows 8% a year pays about 21.7%. In between, the starting ACB sets the level and growth sets the slope.

That has practical consequences. Keeping a careful ACB record matters, because without one an investor may overpay by treating too much of a redemption as gain; the reinvested-distributions guide shows how reinvestments and returns of capital change it. Distributions are taxed every year even when nothing is sold, which is one reason the asset-location guide places the most heavily taxed income in registered accounts where room allows.

06

Planning withdrawals from a non-registered fund

  1. Separate the cash from the tax. Only the gain portion is taxed, but the tax still has to be paid. The sale-proceeds guide earmarks it before spending.
  2. Know which income-tested amounts are affected. Taxable capital gains and fund distributions are part of net income, which income-tested benefits and credits use. The GIS withdrawal-timing guide shows how the source of a withdrawal changes them.
  3. Group redemptions within a year correctly. CRA says multiple redemptions from the same fund in the same year should be grouped together, and each class or series of a fund has its own ACB.
  4. Watch for losses as well as gains. A redemption made while units are below cost realizes a capital loss, which can offset gains under CRA’s rules; this model gives such losses no value. The tax-loss selling guide covers them, including the 30-day rule.
  5. Keep the market risk in view. A lower tax bill does not make a fund safer. Returns are uncertain, a fall early in withdrawals does lasting damage, and the withdrawal-source guide shows how to sell without drifting away from the planned mix.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 26 October 2026. The average-cost rule for identical fund units, the tax on reinvested distributions and the one-half inclusion rate are from CRA pages reviewed 26 October 2026; the 2026 federal and Ontario brackets are from CRA’s 2026 rates page. Balances, growth, distributions and tax rates in the charts are hypothetical editable inputs, not a forecast, the record of any fund or a personal tax calculation. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Canada Revenue Agency · Tax treatment of mutual funds ↗

    Reviewed in the in-app browser on 26 October 2026: distributions are taxed while units are owned, including when reinvested; redemptions are taxed on any gain, usually a capital gain; units of the same class or series are identical properties whose ACB is based on the average cost per unit; multiple redemptions from the same fund in the same year are grouped; each class or series has its own ACB.

  2. Canada Revenue Agency · Calculating and reporting your capital gains and losses ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 for the definitions of deemed disposition and adjusted cost base and the one-half inclusion rate referenced on the page.

  3. Canada Revenue Agency · Current year tax rates and income brackets (2026) ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026. Federal 2026: 14% to CAD 58,523, 20.5% to CAD 117,045, 26% to CAD 181,440, 29% to CAD 258,482, 33% above. Ontario 2026: 5.05% to CAD 53,891, 9.15% to CAD 107,785, then 11.16%, 12.16% and 13.16%.

  4. Canada Revenue Agency · Tax rates on withdrawals (RRSP) ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026: withholding for residents of Canada outside Quebec is 10% up to CAD 5,000, 20% over CAD 5,000 up to CAD 15,000 and 30% over CAD 15,000, and may not cover the final tax.

  5. Canada Revenue Agency · Withdrawing from a TFSA ↗

    Used for the general rule that TFSA withdrawals are not taxable; this page is already cited by earlier TickerLantern TFSA guides.
